name: Athlete body hair removal tradition

lead: Athletes in several sports remove body hair. Competitive swimmers shave legs, arms and torsos; road cyclists and footballers shave legs; bodybuilders remove hair to show muscle definition. Smooth skin also suits the look many associate with athletic bodies.
The practice has deep roots: Wikipedia describes depilation in ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome, where smooth skin was tied to cleanliness and status.

paras: Athletes typically use razors, clippers or hair-removal creams or waxing, often before a meet or competition. Details vary by sport and personal preference.
Risks include nicks, razor burn, irritation and ingrown hairs; skin sensitivity varies between people.

chain: Skin appears smoother, muscle outlines show
angle.text: Removing hair makes muscle shape and skin more visible, a look athletes and bodybuilders use on stage or in sport.

lead: Many athletes remove body hair. Swimmers shave legs, arms and torso to reduce drag and sharpen their feel for the water, while road cyclists and footballers shave legs, which is said to make road rash easier to clean and massage more comfortable.[1] Head shaving is also associated with swimming, bodybuilding and extreme sports.[2]

The idea of smooth skin on the athletic body is old. Wikipedia reports that depilation was common in ancient Egypt among the wealthy of all genders, and that in Greece and Rome men and women removed body hair, linked to cleanliness and status; Greek kouros statues are shown without body hair.[1]
For looks, shaving or trimming shows off muscle definition and a clean line, which bodybuilders and others cite as reasons.[1]

paras: Wikipedia notes that Egyptians used pumice and razors and that Greeks and Romans used depilatories and attendants, with smooth skin associated with purity.[1] Copper razors date to about 3000 BC.[2]

Swimmers shave to reduce drag and improve feel, according to the same overview; cyclists and footballers shave for cleaning wounds and massage, a claim the article notes lacks a citation.[1] Safety razors arrived with King Camp Gillette's 1903 commercial production, and the first razor marketed to women launched in 1916.[1][2]
No studies found in the sources consulted on the tradition as a whole.

timeline.event: Commercial production of the Gillette safety razor begins.[2]
